concepts.explanation: Gravitational field strength at a point is the force per unit mass: g = F/m; numerically equal to the local acceleration due to gravity.

concepts.name: Variation of g with Distance (g_d = GM/d^2)
concepts.explanation: Away from a planet, gravitational field strength decreases with the square of distance from its center: g_d = GM/d^2.

concepts.name: Escape Velocity (v_e = sqrt(2GM/r))
concepts.explanation: Minimum speed needed to escape a celestial body’s gravitational field neglecting air resistance: v_e = √(2GM/r), independent of the projectile’s mass.

concepts.name: Inverse Square Law (Gravitation)
concepts.explanation: The gravitational force magnitude varies inversely with the square of the separation between masses; doubling distance reduces force by a factor of four.

concepts.name: Universal Gravitational Constant (G)
concepts.explanation: The proportionality constant in Newton’s law of gravitation; G ≈ 6.7×10^-11 N m^2 kg^-2, same everywhere in the universe.

concepts.name: Properties of Fluid Pressure
concepts.explanation: In a fluid, pressure increases with depth, acts perpendicular to surfaces, and is isotropic (same in all directions) at a given depth.

concepts.name: Hydrostatic Pressure in Gases
concepts.explanation: For gases of approximately constant density over small height ranges, P ≈ ρgh; in small containers the pressure is nearly uniform.

concepts.name: Measuring Density of Solids and Liquids
concepts.explanation: Determine mass (balance) and volume (geometry or displacement), then compute ρ = m/V.

concepts.name: Determining g from Hydrostatic Pressure Measurements
concepts.explanation: Measure absolute pressure at various depths in a liquid of known density and use g = (P_abs − P_atm)/(ρh) or slope/ρ from P vs h graph.

concepts.name: Unit of Pressure: Pascal (Pa)
concepts.explanation: The SI unit of pressure; 1 Pa = 1 N m^-2.

concepts.name: Pascal in SI Base Units (Pa = kg m^-1 s^-2)
concepts.explanation: Expressing the pascal in base units using 1 N = 1 kg m s^-2 gives 1 Pa = 1 kg m^-1 s^-2.

concepts.name: Density Unit Conversion (g cm^-3 to kg m^-3)
concepts.explanation: Convert using 1 g cm^-3 = 1000 kg m^-3, based on 1 g = 10^-3 kg and 1 cm^3 = 10^-6 m^3.

concepts.name: Gravitational Field Lines Representation
concepts.explanation: Field lines indicate the direction and relative strength of gravitational fields; lines point toward mass and are denser where the field is stronger.

concepts.name: Fluid (Definition)
concepts.explanation: A fluid is a substance that can flow; in physics, this includes liquids and gases.

concepts.name: Work (W = F s)
concepts.explanation: Work done is the product of the component of force along the displacement and the displacement; a scalar quantity measured in joules.

concepts.name: Kinetic Energy (Ek = 1/2 m v^2)
concepts.explanation: The energy a body has due to motion; proportional to mass and the square of speed.

concepts.name: Gravitational Potential Energy (Ep = m g h)
concepts.explanation: Energy due to position in a uniform gravitational field; equals weight times vertical height change.

concepts.name: Power (P = W/t = E/t)
concepts.explanation: Rate at which work is done or energy is converted; a scalar measured in watts.

concepts.name: Percentage Efficiency
concepts.explanation: Ratio of useful power output to power input expressed as a percentage: efficiency = (useful power output / power input) × 100.

concepts.name: Work–Energy Theorem
concepts.explanation: The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy.

concepts.name: Mechanical Energy Conservation in Free Fall
concepts.explanation: In the absence of resistive forces, the sum of kinetic and gravitational potential energy of a freely falling body remains constant.

concepts.name: Elastic Potential Energy
concepts.explanation: Energy stored when an elastic body is stretched or compressed, recoverable as kinetic energy when it returns to its original shape.

concepts.name: Energy Loss in Inelastic Collisions
concepts.explanation: During inelastic collisions, momentum is conserved but total kinetic energy decreases, converting to other forms like heat and sound.

concepts.name: Joule (Unit of Work and Energy)
concepts.explanation: The SI unit of work and energy; 1 J = 1 N m = 1 kg m^2 s^-2.

concepts.name: Watt (Unit of Power) and Base Units
concepts.explanation: The SI unit of power; 1 W = 1 J s^-1 = 1 kg m^2 s^-3.

concepts.name: Path Independence of Gravitational Potential Energy
concepts.explanation: Change in gravitational potential energy depends only on vertical height difference, not on the path taken, reflecting a conservative force field.

concepts.name: Gravitational Potential Energy of Extended Bodies via Center of Mass
concepts.explanation: For extended objects, use the vertical displacement of the center of mass to compute the change in gravitational potential energy.

concepts.name: Average Power
concepts.explanation: Total work or energy transferred divided by the time interval over which it occurs; equals instantaneous power when the rate is constant.

concepts.name: Experiment: Trolley–Falling Mass Energy Conservation
concepts.explanation: Lab procedure using a trolley pulled by a falling mass with motion sensor measurements to show that loss of GPE equals gain in KE for the system.

concepts.name: Renewable and Non-renewable Energy Sources
concepts.explanation: Classification of energy sources by sustainability; renewable sources (e.g., wind, solar) are replenished naturally, unlike fossil fuels.

concepts.name: Uniform Circular Motion
concepts.explanation: Motion at constant speed around a circle where the velocity direction changes continuously; velocity is tangential and acceleration is centripetal.

concepts.name: Tangential (Linear) Speed in Circular Motion
concepts.explanation: Linear speed along the circumference of a circular path; for uniform rotation v = distance per revolution × revolutions per time and relates to angular velocity by v = ω r.

concepts.name: Period of an Orbit
concepts.explanation: Time for one complete revolution around the circular path; for speed v and radius R, T = 2πR / v.

concepts.name: Orbital Speed in a Circular Orbit
concepts.explanation: Speed of a satellite of negligible mass orbiting mass M at radius R given by v^2 = GM / R.

concepts.name: Orbital Period–Radius Relationship (Newtonian Form)
concepts.explanation: Exact relation for circular orbits derived from gravity: T^2 = 4π^2 R^3 / (G M).

concepts.name: Kepler’s Third Law
concepts.explanation: For planets orbiting the Sun, the square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the orbit radius: T^2 ∝ R^3; consistent with Newtonian gravity.

concepts.name: Geostationary Orbit
concepts.explanation: An equatorial, prograde orbit with period 24 hours at a unique altitude (~36,000 km above Earth) such that the satellite remains fixed above one point on Earth.

concepts.name: Apparent Weightlessness in Orbit
concepts.explanation: Astronauts in orbit experience weightlessness because they and their spacecraft are in continuous free fall with the same acceleration in Earth’s gravitational field.

concepts.name: Identifying the Source of Centripetal Force
concepts.explanation: Skill of determining which real force(s) provide the required centripetal force in a scenario (e.g., tension, friction, gravity).

concepts.name: Vertical Circular Motion Tension Analysis
concepts.explanation: Force analysis at top, bottom, and side of a vertical circle using T ± mg = m v^2 / r to find string tension and conditions for maintaining contact.

concepts.name: Low-Earth Orbit (LEO) Characteristics
concepts.explanation: Satellite orbits at ~160–2000 km altitude (often ~800 km), short periods, used for imaging, ISS, and some communications; low latency, high resolution.

concepts.name: Rotational Frequency to Linear Speed Conversion
concepts.explanation: Procedure to convert revolutions per unit time to linear speed using circumference: v = (2πr) × f and T = 1/f.

concepts.name: Elastic Potential Energy in Hookean Systems
concepts.explanation: The work done in stretching or compressing a Hookean object is stored as elastic potential energy: Ep = 1/2 k s^2.

concepts.name: Spring Constant (Elastic Constant) k
concepts.explanation: A proportionality constant in Hooke’s law that relates force to displacement; numerically equal to the slope of the force–extension graph, with units N m^-1.

concepts.name: Restoring Force in Elastic Systems
concepts.explanation: The force exerted by an elastic object that acts to return it to its natural length; equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the applied displacement.

concepts.name: Elasticity (Material Behavior)
concepts.explanation: Property of a material that allows it to return to its original shape and size after the deforming force is removed.

concepts.name: Elastic Limit
concepts.explanation: The maximum deformation beyond which a material will not return to its original shape when the load is removed.

concepts.name: Force–Extension Graph for a Hookean Spring
concepts.explanation: A plot of restoring force F versus extension s that yields a straight line through the origin for a Hookean spring; the slope equals k.

concepts.name: Static Extension of a Vertical Spring (mg = k s)
concepts.explanation: At rest with a hanging mass, the spring’s restoring force balances weight so k s = mg, enabling determination of k, s, or mass.

concepts.name: Equilibrium Position of a Hookean Oscillator
concepts.explanation: The position where the net force on the mass-spring system is zero; motion is oscillations about this point.

concepts.name: Energy Transformations in a Hookean Oscillator
concepts.explanation: Mechanical energy oscillates between kinetic and elastic potential energy; total mechanical energy remains constant (in absence of friction).

concepts.name: Natural Length of a Spring
concepts.explanation: The length of a spring when no external force is applied; used as the reference to measure extension or compression.

concepts.name: Oscillation Cycle (Complete Cycle)
concepts.explanation: One full motion from a starting position through all positions and back to the starting position in periodic motion.

concepts.name: Potential Energy vs Displacement Curve for a Hookean System
concepts.explanation: A parabolic relationship Ep = 1/2 k s^2 symmetric about s = 0, showing how elastic potential energy varies with displacement.

concepts.name: Experimental Verification of Hooke's Law
concepts.explanation: Procedure: measure spring extensions for increasing loads, plot F vs s, observe linearity through the origin, and determine k from the slope.

concepts.name: Sources of Error in Hooke's Law Experiment
concepts.explanation: Common issues include parallax when reading scales, pointer misalignment, and incorrect weight calibration.

concepts.name: Acceleration in a Hookean System
concepts.explanation: From F = -k s and F = m a, the acceleration is a = -(k/m) s, directed toward equilibrium and proportional to displacement.

concepts.name: Negative Sign in Hooke's Law
concepts.explanation: The minus sign in F = -k s indicates that the restoring force acts opposite to the displacement direction.

concepts.name: Celsius Scale of Temperature
concepts.explanation: A practical temperature scale measured in degrees Celsius (°C), often denoted by θ.

concepts.name: Celsius–Kelvin Conversion Formula
concepts.explanation: The relationship θ(°C) = T(K) − 273.15; equivalently T(K) = θ(°C) + 273.15.

concepts.name: Thermometric Property (Definition)
concepts.explanation: Any physical property that changes measurably with temperature and can be used to indicate temperature.

concepts.name: Thermometer (Definition and Principle)
concepts.explanation: An instrument that measures temperature by relating a thermometric property to temperature.

concepts.name: Characteristics of an Ideal Thermometric Property
concepts.explanation: Desirable features include accurate measurability, continuous and linear variation, wide range, high sensitivity, small heat capacity, and fast response.

concepts.name: Liquid-in-Glass Thermometer Principle
concepts.explanation: Uses thermal expansion of a liquid in a capillary; temperature is inferred from the length of the liquid column (e.g., mercury or alcohol).

concepts.name: Electrical Resistance Thermometer (RTD) Principle
concepts.explanation: Relies on the temperature dependence of a conductor’s resistance (typically increasing for metals); resistance is measured to determine temperature.

concepts.name: Thermocouple Thermometer Principle
concepts.explanation: Two dissimilar metals form junctions that produce an emf proportional to the temperature difference; measured with a sensitive voltmeter.

concepts.name: Thermistor (Negative Temperature Coefficient)
concepts.explanation: A semiconductor sensor whose resistance decreases rapidly with small increases in temperature, enabling high sensitivity.

concepts.name: Color as a Thermometric Property (Incandescence)
concepts.explanation: The color of hot objects or certain crystals changes with temperature, enabling remote estimates of high temperatures (e.g., furnaces).

concepts.name: Calibration Curve for a Thermometer
concepts.explanation: A graph of thermometric property versus known temperature used to determine unknown temperatures by interpolation.

concepts.name: Calibration of an Alcohol-in-Glass Thermometer (Experiment)
concepts.explanation: Use melting ice and warmed water with a standard thermometer to record alcohol column lengths at known temperatures and plot length vs temperature.

concepts.name: Sensitivity of a Thermometer
concepts.explanation: The change in the thermometric property per degree change in temperature (slope of the calibration curve).

concepts.name: Reference (Cold) Junction in Thermocouples
concepts.explanation: A junction maintained at a known temperature to convert measured emf into the hot-junction temperature via the temperature difference.

concepts.name: Accuracy vs Precision in Temperature Measurement
concepts.explanation: Accuracy refers to closeness to the true value; precision to repeatability/resolution (e.g., more decimal places improve precision, not necessarily accuracy).

concepts.name: Systematic vs Random Error in Temperature Measurement
concepts.explanation: Systematic errors shift results consistently (e.g., ohmmeter calibration), while random errors cause scatter; both affect thermometer suitability.

concepts.name: Specific heat capacity formula (Q = mcΔθ)
concepts.explanation: Model for heating without phase change: heat added or removed equals mass times specific heat capacity times temperature change.

concepts.name: Specific latent heat formula (Q = m l)
concepts.explanation: Heat for a phase change equals mass times specific latent heat; used at melting/boiling points.

concepts.name: Heat capacity formula (Q = CΔθ)
concepts.explanation: Heat transfer to a body equals its heat capacity times the temperature change.

concepts.name: Phase change at constant temperature
concepts.explanation: During melting or boiling, added or removed heat changes phase while temperature remains constant.

concepts.name: Calorimetry principle (heat lost = heat gained)
concepts.explanation: In an insulated system, total heat lost by hot parts equals total heat gained by cold parts; basis for mixing and phase-change calculations.

concepts.name: Determining specific heat capacity by electrical method
concepts.explanation: Measure electrical energy with a joulemeter while heating a known mass; use Q = mcΔθ accounting for calorimeter and losses.

concepts.name: Determining latent heat of fusion using ice in a calorimeter
concepts.explanation: Add dried ice at 0 °C to warm water, measure masses and temperatures; use energy balance to solve for L and l.

concepts.name: Determining latent heat of vaporisation using steam calorimetry
concepts.explanation: Condense dry steam into cool water in a calorimeter; use measured temperature rise and mass of condensed steam to compute L and l.

concepts.name: Conduction of heat
concepts.explanation: Transfer of heat through a material via molecular or lattice vibrations without bulk motion of the substance.

concepts.name: Emissivity and absorptivity vs surface finish
concepts.explanation: Black, matte surfaces emit and absorb thermal radiation more effectively than bright, shiny surfaces.

concepts.name: U-value (overall heat transfer coefficient)
concepts.explanation: Heat flow rate per square metre per kelvin temperature difference through a building element; unit W m^-2 K^-1.

concepts.name: Heat pump (refrigeration cycle) basics
concepts.explanation: Device that uses work to transfer heat from cold to hot regions via evaporation and condensation of a working fluid.

concepts.name: Heating power-energy-time relation
concepts.explanation: Time to heat equals required energy divided by power input; links P = ΔQ/Δt to calorimetry models.

concepts.name: Experimental verification: Q ∝ Δθ
concepts.explanation: For a fixed mass, heat added is directly proportional to temperature rise; linear Q vs Δθ graph with slope mc or C.

concepts.name: Experimental verification: Q ∝ m
concepts.explanation: For a fixed temperature rise, heat added is directly proportional to mass; linear Q vs m graph with slope cΔθ.

concepts.name: Impact of insulation on energy consumption
concepts.explanation: Reducing U-values of building elements lowers heat loss, decreasing required heating power and improving sustainability.

concepts.name: Sources of error and mitigation in calorimetry
concepts.explanation: Systematic heat losses/gains, thermometer and mass measurement errors; mitigated by insulation, lids, polishing, stirring, and pre-cooling.

concepts.name: Evaporation
concepts.explanation: Surface process where faster molecules escape a liquid below its boiling point; rate increases with temperature.

concepts.name: Travelling wave
concepts.explanation: A disturbance that propagates energy from a source through space or a medium without net transport of matter.

concepts.name: Transverse wave
concepts.explanation: A wave in which particle vibrations are perpendicular to the direction of propagation.

concepts.name: Longitudinal wave
concepts.explanation: A wave in which particle vibrations are parallel to the direction of propagation, featuring compressions and rarefactions.

concepts.name: Frequency–period relationship (T = 1/f)
concepts.explanation: The period is the time for one cycle and equals the reciprocal of frequency.

concepts.name: Energy–amplitude squared relationship
concepts.explanation: For a given wave type, energy transported per unit time is proportional to the square of the amplitude.

concepts.name: Principle of superposition of waves
concepts.explanation: When waves overlap, the resultant displacement equals the algebraic sum of individual displacements at each point.

concepts.name: Interference of waves (constructive and destructive)
concepts.explanation: Combination of waves producing increased amplitude when in phase (constructive) or reduced/cancelled amplitude when out of phase (destructive).

concepts.name: Coherent sources and interference pattern
concepts.explanation: Sources with a constant phase difference and equal frequency produce stable nodal and antinodal patterns.

concepts.name: Node and antinode spacing in standing waves
concepts.explanation: Adjacent nodes or adjacent antinodes are separated by λ/2; a node and next antinode are separated by λ/4.

concepts.name: Doppler effect formula for a moving source
concepts.explanation: Observed frequency from a moving source in a medium: f′ = f c/(c ± u), with minus for approach and plus for recession.

concepts.name: Polarisation of transverse waves
concepts.explanation: Restriction of vibrations to a single plane; only transverse waves can be polarised.

concepts.name: Electromagnetic waves and speed of light (c = fλ)
concepts.explanation: EM waves propagate in vacuum at c ≈ 3.00×10^8 m/s, obeying c = fλ; includes radio to gamma rays.

concepts.name: Sound as a Mechanical Wave
concepts.explanation: Sound propagates via mechanical vibrations in a medium and exhibits reflection, refraction, diffraction, and interference.

concepts.name: Sound as a Longitudinal Wave
concepts.explanation: In sound waves, particles of the medium oscillate parallel to the direction of wave travel, creating compressions and rarefactions.

concepts.name: Pitch–Frequency Relationship
concepts.explanation: Pitch increases with frequency; the frequency of the sound equals the source's vibration frequency.

concepts.name: Loudness–Amplitude Relationship
concepts.explanation: Loudness depends on wave amplitude; larger amplitude corresponds to louder sound.

concepts.name: Wave Speed Equation (Sound): v = fλ
concepts.explanation: The speed of a sound wave equals the product of its frequency and wavelength.

concepts.name: Ultrasound: Definition and Applications
concepts.explanation: Ultrasound refers to sound above 20 kHz; applications include diagnostic imaging, Doppler blood flow, therapy, NDT, sensors, and ultrasonic cleaning.

concepts.name: Interference of Sound and Coherence Requirement
concepts.explanation: Two coherent sound sources produce regions of constructive and destructive interference, leading to spatial loudness variations.

concepts.name: Echoes and Reflection of Sound
concepts.explanation: Reflected sound produces echoes; time-of-flight measurements can be used to determine distances.

concepts.name: Refraction of Sound in the Atmosphere
concepts.explanation: Temperature gradients bend sound rays; warmer air near ground refracts sound upward, cooler layers cause downward refraction.

concepts.name: Harmonics on a Stretched String
concepts.explanation: Allowed standing-wave frequencies are integer multiples of the fundamental (f, 2f, 3f, ...), with additional nodes and antinodes.

concepts.name: Factors Affecting String Fundamental Frequency
concepts.explanation: For a string, f ∝ 1/l, f ∝ √T, and f ∝ 1/√μ, where l is length, T is tension, and μ is mass per unit length.

concepts.name: String Frequency Formula: f = (1/2l)√(T/μ)
concepts.explanation: The fundamental frequency of a stretched string depends on its length, tension, and linear density; dimensionally consistent.

concepts.name: Resonance
concepts.explanation: When a driving frequency matches or is near a system’s natural frequency, large-amplitude oscillations occur.

concepts.name: Natural Frequency of Vibration
concepts.explanation: The characteristic frequency at which a system tends to oscillate when not driven by an external force.

concepts.name: Nodes and Antinodes on a String
concepts.explanation: Nodes are points of zero displacement; antinodes are points of maximum displacement; node-node spacing is λ/2 and node-antinode is λ/4.

concepts.name: Linear Density of a String (μ)
concepts.explanation: Mass per unit length defined by μ = mass/length; a key parameter determining string wave speed and frequency.

concepts.name: Sonometer Verification of String Frequency Model
concepts.explanation: Experimental procedure using a sonometer and tuning forks to verify f = (1/2l)√(T/μ) via resonance and measurements of l, T, and μ.

concepts.name: Sonar Depth Measurement Using Echoes
concepts.explanation: Uses time-of-flight of reflected sound in water with known speed to compute depth (accounting for two-way travel).

concepts.name: Quality (Timbre) of a Musical Note
concepts.explanation: The character of a note depends on the presence and amplitudes of overtones/harmonics in addition to the fundamental.

concepts.name: Young's double-slit interference experiment
concepts.explanation: Monochromatic light passing through two narrow, closely spaced slits produces bright and dark fringes due to interference, providing evidence that light is a wave.

concepts.name: Coherent sources
concepts.explanation: Two wave sources are coherent if they have a constant phase difference and the same frequency, a requirement for stable interference patterns.

concepts.name: Path difference and constructive/destructive interference
concepts.explanation: At a point on a screen, waves interfere constructively when the path difference is an integer multiple of the wavelength and destructively when it is a half-integer multiple.

concepts.name: Young's double-slit formula
concepts.explanation: The angular positions of bright fringes satisfy nλ = d sinθ, with geometry tanθ = x/D linking fringe spacing to screen distance.

concepts.name: Measuring wavelength with Young’s slits
concepts.explanation: Determine λ by measuring fringe spacing and screen distance and using nλ = d sinθ with tanθ = x/D for small angles.

concepts.name: Diffraction grating
concepts.explanation: An optical element with many evenly spaced slits that produces sharp interference maxima due to multi-slit diffraction.

concepts.name: Grating constant and line density relation
concepts.explanation: The slit spacing d equals the reciprocal of the number of lines per millimetre: d (mm) = 1/(lines per mm), convertible to metres.

concepts.name: Diffraction grating formula
concepts.explanation: For normal incidence, the angles of principal maxima satisfy nλ = d sinθ, used for wavelength determination and spectrum analysis.

concepts.name: Maximum diffraction order
concepts.explanation: The highest observable order satisfies n_max = d/λ (since sinθ ≤ 1), determining how many diffracted images appear.

concepts.name: Wavelength measurement using a diffraction grating
concepts.explanation: Measure angles of diffracted orders for a known grating spacing and compute λ from nλ = d sinθ; maximize accuracy with long D and high line density.

concepts.name: Grating dispersion
concepts.explanation: A diffraction grating separates colours because θ in nλ = d sinθ increases with λ for a given order, so red deviates more than violet.

concepts.name: Prism dispersion
concepts.explanation: A prism separates colours because the refractive index varies with wavelength; violet refracts more than red due to higher index.

concepts.name: Wavelength–colour relationship and visible spectrum
concepts.explanation: Visible light spans roughly 3.8×10^-7 m to 7.0×10^-7 m, with perceived colour determined by wavelength; monochromatic light has a single wavelength.

concepts.name: Polarisation as evidence for transverse light
concepts.explanation: Only transverse waves can be polarised; the ability to plane-polarise light demonstrates that light waves are transverse.

concepts.name: Polarising filters and crossed-polariser behavior
concepts.explanation: A polariser transmits light with electric field along its axis; two polarisers transmit maximally when aligned and block light when crossed at 90°.

concepts.name: Polarisation by reflection and glare reduction
concepts.explanation: Reflections from horizontal surfaces are partially horizontally polarised; vertical-axis polarisers (e.g., sunglasses) reduce glare by blocking this component.

concepts.name: Thin-film interference colors
concepts.explanation: Phase differences between reflections from the top and bottom of a thin film cause wavelength-selective constructive interference, producing colours in bubbles and oil films.

concepts.name: Electromagnetic spectrum and wave parameters
concepts.explanation: Electromagnetic waves are transverse, travel at c ≈ 3×10^8 m s^-1 in vacuum, and obey c = fλ; the spectrum spans radio to gamma with overlapping bands and varying ionising ability.

concepts.name: Solar irradiance definition and calculation
concepts.explanation: Solar irradiance I is the power per unit area incident on a surface perpendicular to the Sun’s rays: I = P/A, varying with time, location, and atmospheric conditions.

concepts.name: Ultraviolet bands and biological effects
concepts.explanation: UV radiation is categorized as UVA, UVB, and UVC; UVC is absorbed by the atmosphere, UVB partly absorbed by ozone yet damages DNA and skin, and UVA also contributes to skin damage.

concepts.name: Electric Field (Definition)
concepts.explanation: A region of space where a static charge experiences a non-gravitational force caused by other charges.

concepts.name: Electric Field of a Point Charge
concepts.explanation: Field magnitude due to an isolated point charge: E = (1/(4πɛ0)) (q / r^2), directed radially outward for +q and inward for −q.

concepts.name: Electric Field Lines
concepts.explanation: Diagrammatic representation of electric fields; tangent gives direction of force on a positive test charge, density of lines indicates field strength.

concepts.name: Superposition Principle in Electrostatics
concepts.explanation: The net electrostatic force or field on a charge equals the vector sum of contributions from all other charges.

concepts.name: Permittivity of a Medium
concepts.explanation: A property of the medium (ɛ) that reduces the electrostatic force relative to vacuum; vacuum permittivity ɛ0 ≈ 8.9×10^-12 F m^-1.

concepts.name: Charging by Induction (Procedure)
concepts.explanation: Method to charge an insulated conductor without contact by bringing a charged object nearby, grounding to allow charge flow, then removing ground and the inducing object.

concepts.name: Charging by Friction
concepts.explanation: Transfer of electrons between different materials when rubbed, producing equal and opposite charges (triboelectric effect).

concepts.name: Earthing (Grounding)
concepts.explanation: Connecting a conductor to Earth to allow excess charge to flow, effectively discharging the object.

concepts.name: Surface Charge Distribution on Conductors
concepts.explanation: In electrostatics, charge resides on the outer surface of a conductor, distributes uniformly on a sphere, and accumulates at sharp points.

concepts.name: Point Discharge (Electric Wind)
concepts.explanation: Enhanced field at a sharp point ionizes nearby air; opposite ions neutralize the point while like ions are repelled, producing charge loss and an electric wind.

concepts.name: Polarization and Attraction of Neutral Objects
concepts.explanation: A nearby charge induces charge separation in conductors or molecular polarization in insulators, leading to a net attractive force.

concepts.name: Gold Leaf Electroscope
concepts.explanation: Instrument with a metal cap, stem, and thin gold leaf used to detect charge, estimate relative magnitude, and test for conductors vs insulators; can be charged by induction.

concepts.name: Uniform Electric Field Between Parallel Plates
concepts.explanation: Oppositely charged, parallel plates create an almost uniform electric field in the region between them, with field lines straight and evenly spaced.

concepts.name: Conservation of Electric Charge
concepts.explanation: In any interaction, the algebraic sum of electric charge remains constant; induction produces equal and opposite induced charges.

concepts.name: Lightning Protection via Grounded Conductors
concepts.explanation: Use of lightning rods connected to Earth and discharge wicks on aircraft to safely conduct or leak away accumulated static charge.

concepts.name: Static Electricity Hazards and Mitigation
concepts.explanation: Sparks from static discharge can ignite flammable gases, vapors, or dust; mitigation includes grounding, conductive materials, and controlling sharp points.

concepts.name: Ion (Charged Atom or Molecule)
concepts.explanation: An atom or molecule that has gained or lost electrons, forming positive or negative ions; crucial in air ionization and point discharge phenomena.

concepts.name: Work–Charge–Voltage Relationship (W = qV)
concepts.explanation: The work required to move charge q through a potential difference V is W = qV, equivalently V = W/q.

concepts.name: Volt (Joule per Coulomb)
concepts.explanation: The SI unit of potential difference; 1 volt equals 1 joule of work per coulomb of charge (1 V = 1 J C^-1).

concepts.name: Electric Field Strength–Potential Difference Relation (E = V/d)
concepts.explanation: In a uniform field (e.g., between parallel plates), potential difference equals field strength times separation: V = Ed, so E = V/d.

concepts.name: Unit Equivalence: N C^-1 and V m^-1
concepts.explanation: Demonstration that the SI unit of electric field strength newton per coulomb equals volt per metre (N C^-1 = V m^-1).

concepts.name: Electric Potential at a Point (Relative to Earth)
concepts.explanation: The potential of a point is the potential difference between that point and Earth, taken as zero potential.

concepts.name: Equipotential Conductors in Electrostatic Equilibrium
concepts.explanation: All points on a conductor with static charge are at the same potential; no electric field exists within the conductor.

concepts.name: Conservative Nature of Electrostatic Force (Path Independence)
concepts.explanation: The work done moving a charge between two points in an electrostatic field is independent of the path taken.

concepts.name: Electric Current (Definition)
concepts.explanation: An electric current is a flow of electric charge; in conductors electrons move under the influence of an electric field.

concepts.name: Force on a Charge in an Electric Field (F = qE)
concepts.explanation: A charge q placed in an electric field E experiences a force F = qE.

concepts.name: Energy Gain of Charged Particles Through Potential Difference
concepts.explanation: A charge accelerated through a potential difference V gains kinetic energy ΔKE = qV (equal to the loss of electric potential energy).

concepts.name: Measuring Potential Difference with a Voltmeter
concepts.explanation: Using a voltmeter connected across two points in a circuit to measure the potential difference between them.

concepts.name: Estimating Potential Difference with an Electroscope
concepts.explanation: Using the divergence of an electroscope leaf to estimate the potential difference between a charged conductor and Earth.

concepts.name: Battery Voltage and Terminal Charges (Conceptual Model)
concepts.explanation: A battery maintains excess negative and positive charges on its terminals, creating an electric field; higher voltage implies a stronger field.

concepts.name: Charge-Current-Time Relationship (q = It)
concepts.explanation: For a steady current, the charge passing a point equals current times time: q = I t.

concepts.name: Electric Charge
concepts.explanation: A property of matter that causes electrostatic forces; exists as positive and negative and is carried by particles such as electrons and protons.

concepts.name: Ampere (Unit of Electric Current)
concepts.explanation: The SI unit of current, A; defined as 1 coulomb of charge passing per second (1 A = 1 C s^-1).

concepts.name: Elementary Charge (Charge of an Electron)
concepts.explanation: The magnitude of the charge on one electron or proton, e = 1.6×10^-19 C.

concepts.name: Electron Flow in Metal Conductors
concepts.explanation: In metals, mobile electrons drift through the lattice, constituting the electric current.

concepts.name: Conservation of Electric Charge in Circuits
concepts.explanation: Charge does not appear or disappear in a circuit; the same amount entering a region per second must leave it.

concepts.name: Kirchhoff's Current Law (Junction Rule)
concepts.explanation: At any junction, the sum of currents entering equals the sum of currents leaving.

concepts.name: Current in Series Circuits
concepts.explanation: In a single-path (series) circuit, the current is the same at every point.

concepts.name: Current in Parallel Circuits
concepts.explanation: In parallel branches, current splits among paths; the branch currents sum to the total current.

concepts.name: Conventional Current Direction
concepts.explanation: By convention, current is taken to flow from the positive terminal to the negative terminal, opposite to electron flow in metals.

concepts.name: Direct Current (DC)
concepts.explanation: An electric current that flows in one direction only, as from cells or batteries.

concepts.name: Ammeter Connection and Use
concepts.explanation: To measure current, break the circuit and insert the ammeter in series with the component; reading is the same anywhere in a series path.

concepts.name: Electrical Conductor
concepts.explanation: A material that allows electric charge to flow, e.g., metals and electrolytes.

concepts.name: Electrical Insulator
concepts.explanation: A material that resists the flow of electric charge, e.g., plastic, glass, rubber.

concepts.name: Effects of Electric Current
concepts.explanation: Observable effects include heating, magnetic fields around conductors, and chemical reactions in electrolytes.

concepts.name: Electric Circuit
concepts.explanation: A closed path that allows electric charge to flow; can be arranged in series or parallel.

concepts.name: Battery Polarity and Circuit Symbol
concepts.explanation: In the battery symbol, the longer thin line denotes the positive terminal and the shorter thick line the negative terminal.

concepts.name: Galvanometer
concepts.explanation: A sensitive current meter (milliammeter or microammeter) for measuring small currents.

concepts.name: Potential Difference (Voltage)
concepts.explanation: The energy lost or gained per coulomb of charge between two points in a circuit; V = W/q and 1 V = 1 J C^-1.

concepts.name: Electric Power in Circuits (P = VI)
concepts.explanation: Rate of electrical energy conversion in a component equals the product of potential difference and current; P = VI, with power also given by P = W/t.

concepts.name: Voltages in Series (Sum of Potential Differences)
concepts.explanation: Across consecutive series elements, the total potential difference equals the sum of the individual drops: V = V1 + V2 + V3.

concepts.name: Voltages in Parallel (Equal Potential Difference)
concepts.explanation: All branches connected in parallel share the same potential difference: V1 = V2 = V3.

concepts.name: Electromotive Force (emf)
concepts.explanation: The source-applied voltage that supplies electrical potential energy per coulomb to charges in a source; symbol E, unit volt.

concepts.name: Series Combination of Cells (emfs Add)
concepts.explanation: When cells are connected + to − in series, their emfs add to give the total applied voltage.

concepts.name: Energy Transformations in a Simple Electric Circuit
concepts.explanation: Chemical energy in a source becomes electrical potential energy of charges, which is then converted to heat (and sometimes light or mechanical energy) in components.

concepts.name: Path Independence of Electric Potential Difference
concepts.explanation: The change in electric potential energy between two points in an electrostatic field is independent of the path taken (conservative field).

concepts.name: Watt (Unit of Power)
concepts.explanation: The SI unit of power; 1 watt equals 1 joule per second (1 W = 1 J s^-1).

concepts.name: Electric Current as Rate of Charge Flow (I = q/t)
concepts.explanation: Current is the rate at which charge passes a point: I = q/t, used to relate power and voltage in circuits.

concepts.name: Electrical Resistance (R = V/I)
concepts.explanation: Resistance is the ratio of potential difference across a conductor to the current through it; a scalar with SI unit ohm (Ω).

concepts.name: Ohmic Conductor
concepts.explanation: A conductor whose resistance remains constant with changing V and I at constant temperature; exhibits a linear I–V graph through the origin.

concepts.name: Resistivity (ρ) and R = ρl/A
concepts.explanation: Material property linking resistance to geometry: R equals resistivity times length over cross-sectional area; SI unit is ohm metre (Ω m).

concepts.name: Equivalent Resistance: Series
concepts.explanation: For resistors in series, the total resistance is the sum of individual resistances: Req = R1 + R2 + ....

concepts.name: Equivalent Resistance: Parallel
concepts.explanation: For resistors in parallel, the reciprocal of the total resistance is the sum of reciprocals: 1/Req = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ....

concepts.name: Potential Divider (Voltage Division)
concepts.explanation: Two (or more) series resistors divide a supply voltage; the voltage across a resistor is proportional to its resistance (e.g., Vout = Vs·R2/(R1+R2)).

concepts.name: Variable Potential Divider (Potentiometer)
concepts.explanation: A resistive element with a sliding contact provides a continuously adjustable output voltage from 0 to the supply voltage.

concepts.name: Resistance–Length Proportionality
concepts.explanation: For a uniform conductor of fixed cross-sectional area, resistance is directly proportional to its length (R ∝ l).

concepts.name: Resistance–Area Inverse Proportionality
concepts.explanation: For a uniform conductor of fixed length, resistance is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area (R ∝ 1/A).

concepts.name: Temperature Dependence of Metal Resistance
concepts.explanation: In metals, resistance increases with temperature due to increased lattice vibrations; approximately linear for moderate temperature changes.

concepts.name: Thermistor (NTC) Behavior
concepts.explanation: A semiconductor device whose resistance decreases rapidly with increasing temperature; exhibits a nonlinear R–T characteristic.

concepts.name: Temperature Dependence in Semiconductors and Insulators
concepts.explanation: R decreases with temperature as more charge carriers are thermally generated, outweighing increased lattice scattering.

concepts.name: Measuring Resistance with Ammeter and Voltmeter
concepts.explanation: Connect ammeter in series and voltmeter in parallel, measure I and V, then compute R = V/I.

concepts.name: Variable Resistor (Rheostat) Operation
concepts.explanation: A two-terminal adjustable resistor used to vary current or resistance in a circuit by changing the conductor length in use.

concepts.name: Experimental Verification of Ohm's Law
concepts.explanation: Vary the voltage across a resistance wire, measure I and V, plot I vs V; a straight line through the origin confirms ohmic behavior; minimize heating and use proper meter placement.

concepts.name: Experimental Study of Series and Parallel Resistor Combinations
concepts.explanation: Measure individual and combined resistances with an ohmmeter; compare with theoretical series and parallel formulas to validate circuit rules.

concepts.name: Experiment: Metal Resistance vs Temperature
concepts.explanation: Measure a coil’s resistance at multiple temperatures in a thermal bath (e.g., glycerol), plot R vs T, observe approximately linear increase; control heating rate and stir for uniform temperature.

concepts.name: Experiment: Thermistor Resistance vs Temperature
concepts.explanation: Measure a thermistor’s resistance across a temperature range in a thermal bath, plot R vs T, observe strong decrease; manage lead resistance and temperature uniformity.

concepts.name: Electrical Power in DC Circuits (P = VI, P = I^2 R, P = V^2/R)
concepts.explanation: Power is the rate of energy conversion; using V = IR leads to equivalent forms to model dissipation and device ratings.

concepts.name: Non-Ohmic Behavior of Filament Lamps
concepts.explanation: A filament bulb has a non-linear I–V relationship because its resistance increases with temperature as current and voltage rise.

concepts.name: I–V Measurement Procedure for a Filament Lamp
concepts.explanation: Vary the voltage with a variable resistor, measure current and voltage with ammeter and voltmeter (in series/parallel respectively), and plot I versus V to obtain the characteristic curve.

concepts.name: High-Voltage Power Transmission to Minimize I^2R Losses
concepts.explanation: Stepping up voltage reduces current for a given power, lowering resistive losses in transmission lines (P_loss = I^2 R).

concepts.name: Transformers in the Grid (Step-Up and Step-Down)
concepts.explanation: Transformers raise voltage for transmission and lower it for safe domestic use, enabling efficient power delivery.

concepts.name: Protective Earthing of Appliances
concepts.explanation: Connecting exposed metal parts to earth provides a low-resistance fault path, causing overcurrent protection to operate and keeping casings at zero potential.

concepts.name: Fuses: Melting Wire Overcurrent Protection in Live Conductor
concepts.explanation: A fuse melts when current exceeds its rating, breaking the circuit; it must be placed in the live conductor to isolate the appliance from the supply.

concepts.name: Selecting Fuse Ratings from Appliance Power and Supply Voltage
concepts.explanation: Determine appliance current using I = P/V and choose the next appropriate standard fuse rating to ensure protection without nuisance blowing.

concepts.name: Miniature Circuit Breakers (MCBs): Thermal-Magnetic Trip
concepts.explanation: MCBs trip via a bimetal strip for overloads and a solenoid for short circuits; they act faster than fuses and can be reset.

concepts.name: Residual Current Devices (RCDs): Differential Current Protection (≈30 mA, <30 ms)
concepts.explanation: RCDs detect differences between live and neutral currents and trip rapidly at small imbalances to reduce shock risk; they do not protect against live-neutral contact.

concepts.name: Switch Placement in Live Conductor for Safe Isolation
concepts.explanation: Switches must interrupt the live conductor so that the appliance is disconnected from dangerous potential when off.

concepts.name: Live, Neutral, and Earth Conductors: Roles and Color Codes
concepts.explanation: Live carries alternating high potential (brown), neutral is near earth potential (blue), and earth is protective (green/yellow); correct identification is essential for safety.

concepts.name: Kilowatt-hour (kWh) as an Energy Unit and Conversion to Joules
concepts.explanation: 1 kWh is the energy used by a 1 kW device in 1 hour; 1 kWh = 3.6 MJ; used in electricity billing.

concepts.name: Percentage Efficiency of Electrical Devices
concepts.explanation: Efficiency = (useful output power / input power) × 100%; used to evaluate device performance and losses.

concepts.name: Correct Connection of Meters: Ammeter in Series, Voltmeter in Parallel
concepts.explanation: For accurate measurements, place the ammeter in series to measure current and the voltmeter in parallel across components to measure potential difference.

concepts.name: Electrocution Risk and Current Path Through the Body
concepts.explanation: The human body conducts electricity; shock severity depends on current path (e.g., across the chest is most dangerous); insulation increases resistance but is not fail-safe.

concepts.name: Ring Main Circuit for Sockets
concepts.explanation: Sockets are often wired in a ring with live and neutral loops so each outlet is supplied from both sides; the ring is protected by a fuse/MCB in the live.

concepts.name: Parallel Lighting Circuits in Homes
concepts.explanation: Domestic lights are wired in parallel with individual live switches so that failure of one lamp does not affect others and each receives full supply voltage.

concepts.name: Semiconductor
concepts.explanation: A material with resistivity between a conductor and an insulator; its resistivity decreases as temperature increases.

concepts.name: Intrinsic conduction in semiconductors
concepts.explanation: Electrical conduction in a pure semiconductor due to thermally generated electron–hole pairs moving in opposite directions.

concepts.name: Doping (semiconductors)
concepts.explanation: The controlled addition of small amounts of impurities to a pure semiconductor to increase its conductivity.

concepts.name: Extrinsic conduction in semiconductors
concepts.explanation: Enhanced conduction in a doped semiconductor due to majority carriers introduced by impurities.

concepts.name: n-type semiconductor
concepts.explanation: A doped semiconductor (e.g., Si with P) where electrons are the majority charge carriers.

concepts.name: p-type semiconductor
concepts.explanation: A doped semiconductor (e.g., Si with B) where holes are the majority charge carriers.

concepts.name: Majority and minority charge carriers
concepts.explanation: In doped semiconductors, majority carriers are introduced by the dopant; the opposite type from intrinsic generation are minority carriers.

concepts.name: Positive hole (charge carrier)
concepts.explanation: An effective positive charge representing the absence of an electron in a covalent bond that moves through the lattice.

concepts.name: p-n junction
concepts.explanation: An interface formed by joining p-type and n-type regions in a single crystal, central to diode and transistor operation.

concepts.name: Depletion layer
concepts.explanation: A region near the p-n junction depleted of free majority carriers, acting as an insulator.

concepts.name: Junction voltage (built-in potential)
concepts.explanation: The potential difference across a p-n junction due to charge separation during formation (≈0.6 V for Si, ≈0.2 V for Ge).

concepts.name: Forward bias of a p-n junction
concepts.explanation: Biasing with positive to p-type and negative to n-type reduces the depletion barrier and allows significant current flow.

concepts.name: Reverse bias of a p-n junction (leakage and breakdown)
concepts.explanation: Biasing with positive to n-type and negative to p-type widens the depletion region; only tiny leakage current flows until breakdown at high voltage.

concepts.name: I–V characteristic of a semiconductor diode
concepts.explanation: Nonlinear relationship where current rises sharply past the junction voltage in forward bias and remains near zero in reverse bias until breakdown.

concepts.name: Rectification using a diode
concepts.explanation: Conversion of AC to pulsating DC by allowing current during one half-cycle and blocking the other.

concepts.name: Light-emitting diode (LED): operation
concepts.explanation: A forward-biased p-n junction where electron–hole recombination emits photons; brightness depends on current.

concepts.name: LED color determined by bandgap
concepts.explanation: Photon energy (and thus color) equals the semiconductor bandgap; varies with material composition.

concepts.name: Series current-limiting resistor for diodes/LEDs
concepts.explanation: A resistor in series sets safe current through a diode by limiting current when supply voltage exceeds diode drop.

concepts.name: Light-dependent resistor (LDR) behavior
concepts.explanation: A photoconductive semiconductor whose resistance decreases with increasing light intensity.

concepts.name: npn junction transistor (structure and terminals)
concepts.explanation: A three-layer device with n–p–n regions forming emitter, base, and collector; two p-n junctions within one crystal.

concepts.name: Common-emitter configuration
concepts.explanation: Transistor circuit where the emitter is common to input and output; used for switching and amplification.

concepts.name: Transistor current relation (Ie = Ic + Ib)
concepts.explanation: In a BJT, emitter current equals the sum of collector and base currents by charge conservation.

concepts.name: Transistor as an electronic switch
concepts.explanation: A small base current (or voltage) controls a much larger collector current, enabling on/off control via sensors and potential dividers.

concepts.name: Experiment: Measuring I–V characteristics of a diode
concepts.explanation: Procedure to record current vs voltage in forward and reverse bias using appropriate meters and series resistance, producing a characteristic curve.

concepts.name: Non-ohmic behavior of a diode
concepts.explanation: A diode does not obey Ohm’s law; its resistance is not constant and current depends nonlinearly on applied voltage.

concepts.name: Magnetic field
concepts.explanation: A region of space where magnetic forces can be felt; direction at a point is the force direction on a test north pole placed there.

concepts.name: Magnetic field lines
concepts.explanation: Lines used to represent magnetic fields; they point from north to south, their density indicates field strength, and they never cross.

concepts.name: Magnetic poles
concepts.explanation: Magnets have north and south poles that occur in pairs with equal strength; poles are regions where magnetic effects are strongest.

concepts.name: Forces between magnetic poles
concepts.explanation: Like poles repel and unlike poles attract; the force increases as poles are brought closer and decreases with distance.

concepts.name: Ferromagnetism
concepts.explanation: Property of materials like iron, nickel, and cobalt that are strongly attracted by magnets and can be magnetized.

concepts.name: Induced magnetism
concepts.explanation: Temporary or permanent magnetization of a ferromagnetic material when placed in a magnetic field or in contact with a magnet.

concepts.name: Permanent and temporary magnets
concepts.explanation: Permanent magnets retain magnetization; temporary magnets lose most or all magnetization when the magnetizing field is removed.

concepts.name: Magnetic effect of an electric current
concepts.explanation: A current-carrying conductor produces a magnetic field that exists only while current flows; direction depends on current direction.

concepts.name: Magnetic field of a straight current-carrying wire
concepts.explanation: The field consists of concentric circles around the wire; strength increases with current and decreases with distance from the wire.

concepts.name: Right-hand grip rule
concepts.explanation: If the right hand grasps a conductor with the thumb pointing in the direction of conventional current, curled fingers show the field direction.

concepts.name: Determining solenoid polarity from current direction
concepts.explanation: Looking into a coil, clockwise current gives a south pole and anticlockwise current gives a north pole at the facing end.

concepts.name: Electromagnet
concepts.explanation: A soft iron core inside a current-carrying solenoid produces a strong magnetic field; magnetism is switchable with the current.

concepts.name: Effect of ferrous core on solenoid field strength
concepts.explanation: Inserting a ferromagnetic core into a solenoid greatly increases the magnetic field strength due to magnetization of the core.

concepts.name: Mapping magnetic fields with a plotting compass
concepts.explanation: Procedure: step the compass so one pole follows previous marks to trace field lines and their direction around magnets or currents.

concepts.name: Visualizing magnetic fields with iron filings
concepts.explanation: Sprinkled filings align along field lines on a card over magnets or current-carrying conductors to reveal field patterns qualitatively.

concepts.name: Magnetic compass operation
concepts.explanation: A small bar magnet that aligns with the local magnetic field; used to determine field direction and for navigation.

concepts.name: Motor Effect
concepts.explanation: A current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field experiences a force perpendicular to both the current and the field, and zero force if parallel to the field.

concepts.name: Fleming's Left-Hand Rule
concepts.explanation: With thumb, first finger, and second finger mutually perpendicular: first finger points in field direction, second in conventional current, thumb gives force direction on the conductor.

concepts.name: Force on a Moving Charge in a Magnetic Field (F = B q v)
concepts.explanation: A charge q moving with speed v at right angles to a magnetic field B experiences a force F = B q v, perpendicular to both velocity and field; zero if velocity is parallel to the field.
concepts.broader_concept: Charged Particle Dynamics in Magnetic Fields

concepts.name: Circular Motion of Charged Particles in Uniform Magnetic Fields
concepts.explanation: When v ⟂ B, the magnetic force acts as the centripetal force so that m v^2 / r = B q v, giving a circular path with radius r = m v / (B q).
concepts.broader_concept: Charged Particle Dynamics in Magnetic Fields

concepts.name: Tesla (T) as SI Unit of Magnetic Flux Density
concepts.explanation: 1 tesla is the magnetic flux density that produces a force of 1 N on a 1 m length of conductor carrying 1 A perpendicular to the field; base units kg s^-2 A^-1.

concepts.name: Torque on a Current Loop in a Magnetic Field (Qualitative)
concepts.explanation: Opposite forces on the sides of a current-carrying coil in a uniform magnetic field create a turning effect that varies with orientation; the torque reduces and can be zero at specific angles.

concepts.name: Split-Ring Commutator
concepts.explanation: A rotating split ring that reverses the current in the coil every half turn in a DC motor, maintaining continuous rotation by keeping the torque direction consistent.

concepts.name: Force Between Parallel Current-Carrying Conductors
concepts.explanation: Parallel currents in the same direction attract; in opposite directions repel, due to interaction of their magnetic fields; directions can be predicted with the left-hand rule.

concepts.name: Experimental Determination of Magnetic Flux Density Using F–I Graphs
concepts.explanation: Measure force on a wire of known length in a uniform field while varying current; plot F versus I; slope equals B l, allowing calculation of B and exploration of direction effects.

concepts.name: Cathode Ray Deflection by a Magnetic Field
concepts.explanation: Electron beams act as moving charges and are deflected by magnetic fields; deflection direction depends on field polarity and is predicted by the left-hand rule (with charge sign considered).
concepts.broader_concept: Force on a Moving Charge in a Magnetic Field

concepts.name: Dimensional Verification of m v^2 / r = B q v
concepts.explanation: Confirming the magnetic-radius formula by equating base units on both sides to ensure dimensional consistency (kg m s^-2).

concepts.name: Electromagnetic Induction (Generator Effect)
concepts.explanation: A changing magnetic field (changing magnetic flux through a conductor) induces an emf in the conductor, which can drive a current if the circuit is closed.

concepts.name: Magnetic Flux (Φ)
concepts.explanation: The total magnetic field passing through an area: Φ = B⊥ A (component of B perpendicular to the area times area). SI unit is the weber (Wb), where 1 Wb = 1 T·m².

concepts.name: Conditions for Induced EMF and Current
concepts.explanation: An emf is induced only when the magnetic flux through a coil changes; a current flows only if the circuit is complete. An emf is induced even in an open circuit.

concepts.name: Simple AC Generator (Alternator)
concepts.explanation: A rotating coil in a uniform magnetic field produces a sinusoidal emf; slip rings connect the rotating coil to the external circuit so the current alternates.

concepts.name: Simple DC Generator
concepts.explanation: A rotating coil with a split-ring commutator produces unidirectional (pulsating) current by reversing connections each half-turn so current in the external circuit does not change direction.

concepts.name: Slip Rings
concepts.explanation: Rotating conductive rings that maintain continuous electrical contact between a spinning coil and external circuit, enabling AC output in generators.

concepts.name: Alternating Current (AC) Fundamentals
concepts.explanation: In AC circuits, current reverses direction periodically with frequency f (e.g., 50 Hz). Sinusoidal waveforms describe voltage and current vs time.

concepts.name: RMS and Peak Values for Sinusoidal AC
concepts.explanation: RMS values equate AC heating effect to DC: Irms = I0/√2 and Vrms = V0/√2 for sinusoidal waveforms.

concepts.name: Average Power in a Resistive AC Circuit
concepts.explanation: For a pure resistor, average power P = Irms Vrms = Irms² R, analogous to DC but using RMS values.

concepts.name: Oscilloscope Display of AC and DC
concepts.explanation: AC across the Y-plates with a suitable time base displays a sinusoidal trace; DC produces a horizontal line at a fixed deflection.

concepts.name: Mutual Inductance
concepts.explanation: A changing current in one coil induces an emf in a nearby coil via the shared changing magnetic flux; increased by closer coupling, shared soft-iron core, and more turns.

concepts.name: Transformer Principle
concepts.explanation: Two coils on a soft iron core use mutual inductance to change AC voltage: alternating flux from the primary induces an emf in the secondary.

concepts.name: Transformer Turns Ratio
concepts.explanation: For an ideal transformer, the voltage ratio equals the turns ratio: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np, enabling step-up or step-down operation.

concepts.name: Ideal Transformer Power Relation
concepts.explanation: Assuming no losses, input power equals output power: Ip Vp = Is Vs, linking currents and voltages between windings.

concepts.name: Transformer Efficiency and Energy Losses
concepts.explanation: Real transformers lose energy via I²R heating, eddy currents, hysteresis in the core, and flux leakage; lamination reduces eddy currents, soft iron minimizes hysteresis loss.

concepts.name: Eddy Currents and Magnetic Damping
concepts.explanation: Changing magnetic fields in conductors induce circulating currents that oppose motion (e.g., a magnet falling in a copper tube), producing damping forces.

concepts.name: High-Voltage Power Transmission to Reduce I²R Losses
concepts.explanation: Stepping up voltage for transmission reduces current and hence resistive (I²R) heating losses in long-distance power lines.

concepts.name: Einstein's photoelectric equation
concepts.explanation: Relates photon energy to emitted electron kinetic energy: hf = φ + 1/2 m v_max^2, explaining threshold behavior and dependence on frequency, not intensity.

concepts.name: Threshold frequency (f0)
concepts.explanation: Minimum frequency of incident radiation required to cause photoemission from a given metal; below f0 no electrons are emitted regardless of intensity.

concepts.name: Photon energy (E = hf and E = hc/λ)
concepts.explanation: Energy of a photon is proportional to frequency (E = hf) and inversely proportional to wavelength (E = hc/λ), introducing quantization of light.

concepts.name: Photocell operation and photocurrent–intensity relationship
concepts.explanation: In a vacuum photocell, light above threshold causes emission of photoelectrons collected at the anode; the photocurrent is directly proportional to light intensity.

concepts.name: Electron properties and elementary charge quantization
concepts.explanation: Electron has mass 9.11×10^-31 kg and charge −1.602×10^-19 C; electric charge is quantized in integer multiples of the elementary charge.

concepts.name: Cathode rays
concepts.explanation: Streams of high-speed electrons emitted from the cathode in a vacuum tube, producing fluorescence and deflecting in electric and magnetic fields.

concepts.name: Cathode ray tube (CRT) operation
concepts.explanation: Electrons thermionically emitted from a heated cathode are accelerated by an anode voltage to form a beam that produces fluorescence on a screen; deflection plates steer the beam.

concepts.name: Energy gained by an electron in a potential difference (W = qV; eV = 1/2 mv^2)
concepts.explanation: An electron accelerated through voltage V gains kinetic energy eV, equating electric potential energy loss to kinetic energy gain.
concepts.broader_concept: Motion of Charges in Electric Fields

concepts.name: Electronvolt (eV) and unit conversions
concepts.explanation: Energy unit equal to the work done when an electron moves through 1 volt: 1 eV = 1.602×10^-19 J; includes keV, MeV, GeV scales.

concepts.name: Deflection of electrons in an electric field
concepts.explanation: Electron beams deflect opposite to electric field lines between charged plates; magnitude of deflection increases with potential difference.
concepts.broader_concept: Motion of Charged Particles in Fields

concepts.name: Circular motion of electrons in a uniform magnetic field
concepts.explanation: A perpendicular, constant-magnitude magnetic force provides centripetal force, giving radius r = mv/(qB) for an electron’s circular path.

concepts.name: Predicting electron beam deflection using Fleming's left-hand rule
concepts.explanation: Determines the direction of force on a current (or electron beam) in a magnetic field by orienting thumb, first, and second fingers for force, field, and current respectively.
concepts.broader_concept: Motion of Charged Particles in Fields

concepts.name: Thomson’s e/m measurement for the electron
concepts.explanation: Using crossed electric and magnetic fields to balance deflections of cathode rays, Thomson determined the electron’s charge-to-mass ratio and identified cathode rays as electrons.

concepts.name: X-ray production in a hot cathode tube
concepts.explanation: High-speed electrons accelerated by a large anode voltage strike a metal target; a small fraction of their kinetic energy is converted into X-rays, with heat removal and shielding required.

concepts.name: Minimum X-ray wavelength from tube voltage (λ_min = hc/eV)
concepts.explanation: The shortest possible X-ray wavelength occurs if an electron’s full kinetic energy eV converts to a single photon: λ_min = hc/(eV).

concepts.name: Comparing X-ray production and the photoelectric effect
concepts.explanation: Contrasts electrons-in/radiation-out (X-rays) with radiation-in/electrons-out (photoelectric); highlights threshold criteria and different dependencies on frequency and intensity.

concepts.name: Photocurrent–distance inverse-square experiment
concepts.explanation: By varying source distance and plotting photocurrent versus 1/d^2, verifies photocurrent ∝ light intensity via the inverse-square law.

concepts.name: Photomultiplier tube principle
concepts.explanation: Single photoelectron is accelerated to dynodes causing secondary emission cascades, amplifying weak light signals into measurable currents.

concepts.name: Relating photocurrent to electron rate and photon flux
concepts.explanation: Photocurrent I gives electron count rate I/e; assuming one photon emits one electron, photon flux equals electron rate, enabling optical power estimates via E = hf.
